summary: This comprehensive review examines integrated superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (iSNSPDs), covering their operational principles, performance metrics, material platforms, and integration strategies for quantum photonic systems. State-of-the-art iSNSPDs achieve on-chip detection efficiency exceeding 99% at telecom wavelengths, dark count rates below 0.0001 Hz, sub-500 ps recovery times, and timing jitter below 15 ps, with demonstrated photon-number resolution up to 100 photons.
motivation: Scalable quantum photonics requires integration of single-photon detectors with photonic circuits to minimize losses and enable multichannel detection, yet previous reviews have not comprehensively addressed the rapidly evolving field of integrated SNSPDs, particularly recent advances in device architectures, material engineering, and integration strategies.
method: The review systematically analyzes iSNSPD working principles across multiple theoretical models (hotspot, vortex, vortex-antivortex pair mechanisms), characterizes performance metrics and their dependencies on nanowire geometry and material properties, evaluates superconducting materials (NbN, NbTiN, WSi, MoSi) and photonic platforms (SOI, SiN, LNOI, GaAs, diamond), and discusses photon-number-resolving implementations.
result: Record iSNSPDs demonstrate simultaneous high performance: on-chip detection efficiency of $99.73\%$ at 1550 nm, recovery time of 120 ps, jitter of 12.2 ps, and dark count rates reaching $10^{-4}$ Hz; integration with active photonic components (sources, modulators) has been demonstrated across multiple platforms, though scalability challenges remain in array uniformity, thermal management, and the fundamental absorption-speed-loss tradeoff.
